newsitem.title: FRANCE: French experts propose simpler immigration, asylum.
newsitem.headline: French experts propose simpler immigration, asylum.

text.p: A team of specialists unveiled on Thursday a government-commissioned report suggesting ways to simplify and "humanise" France's complicated and stringent immigration and asylum laws.

The report was handed to Prime Minister Lionel Jospin by the team's chief, sociologist Patrick Weil, who later told a news conference those suggestions approved by the government would be submitted to parliament in the fall.
Weil said French policy would still be to prevent new mass waves of non-qualified immigrants from settling in France.

There are about five million foreign nationals already in France, including about a million who are here illegally. Most new arrivals are from Africa and Asia and have had more difficulty integrating than earlier generations of immigrants such as Spaniards, Italians or Poles.

The immigrants' adjustment difficulties and many French people's rejection of them at a time of high unemployment have fuelled the electoral rise of rightist Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front which wants to expel them.

Weil said his proposals were aimed at simplifying entry for third world businessmen and bona fida students, who he said were turning to Anglo-Saxon countries for trade or educational links because of problems getting into France.
"Today, we impose pettiness on those whom we should accept among us, but do not bother enough those who should not come," Weil said.

Weil proposed overhauling asylum laws to exclude East Europeans whose regimes were now democratic, but opening borders to Algerians persecuted by Islamic fundamentalist groups. Only people persecuted by governments are now eligible for asylum.
Weil's report was presented as the government separately prepared to legalise up to 40,000 illegal immigrants, many of them black Africans, who are in legal limbo because of changes in legislation.
Weil denied that Paris wanted to impose a "social" bar to third world immigrants -- rather than a colour bar -- that would exclude the poor but attract rich elites from developing countries.
The report referred several times to fears that France's influence in Africa would be overtaken by that of the United States, a thought that is a near-obsession of some French officials.
Although aimed at simplifying laws, Weil's proposals numbered 130 and some appeared far more complicated than the laws they aimed at replacing.
